The clinical and health subject ranking uses the same trusted and rigorous performance indicators as the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2023, but the methodology has been recalibrated to suit the individual fields.

It highlights the universities that are leading across medicine, dentistry and other health subjects.

This year’s table includes 1,001 universities, up from 925 last year.

View the World University Rankings 2023 by subject: clinical and health methodology

The UK’s University of Oxford leads the table for the 12th consecutive year, with just two universities in the top 10 not from the US or the UK. These – China’s Tsinghua University and Canada’s University of Toronto – have swapped positions from last year. Tsinghua University is now in fifth place and the University of Toronto in seventh.

The **Russell Group** is a self-selected association of twenty-four [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"). The group is headquartered in [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge "Cambridge") and was established in 1994 to represent its members' interests, principally to [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom") and [parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom "Parliament of the United Kingdom"). It was incorporated in 2007.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-About-3) Its members are often perceived as being the UK's best universities, which has been widely disputed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-4)

As of 2017,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit) Russell Group members receive over three-quarters of all university research grant and contract income in the United Kingdom.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-profile-5) Russell Group members award 60% of all doctorates gained in the United Kingdom.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-profile-5) In the 2021 [Research Excellence Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Excellence_Framework "Research Excellence Framework"), Russell Group universities accounted for 65% of all world-leading (4*) research conducted in the UK, and 91% of the Russell Group's research was judged to be world-leading (4*) or internationally excellent (3*).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-6) In the 2023 [Teaching Excellence and Student Outcomes Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teaching_Excellence_Framework "Teaching Excellence Framework") (TEF), of the 20 English Russell Group universities which were assessed, 7 hold gold awards (35%) and 13 silver (65%). This compares to proportions across 128 higher education institutions of which 29% hold gold, 62% silver, and 9% bronze.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-7) Their graduates hold 61% of all UK jobs that require a university degree, despite being only 17% of all higher education graduates.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-9)

The Russell Group is named after the location of the first informal meetings of the Group, which took place at the [Hotel Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimpton_Fitzroy_London_Hotel "Kimpton Fitzroy London Hotel") in [Russell Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Square "Russell Square"), London.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-bbc12312-10)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Russell Group of universities was formed in 1994 by 17 British research universities – Birmingham, Bristol, Cambridge, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Imperial College London, Leeds, Liverpool, London School of Economics, Manchester, Newcastle, Nottingham, Oxford, Sheffield, Southampton, University College London and Warwick, who originally met at [Hotel Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotel_Russell "Hotel Russell") shortly before meetings of the Committee of Vice-Chancellors and Principals (now [Universities UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_UK "Universities UK")) in nearby [Tavistock Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tavistock_Square "Tavistock Square"), close to the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London") buildings and, particularly, [Senate House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_House_(University_of_London) "Senate House (University of London)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-bbc12312-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-guardian2012-11) With the exception of [Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick "University of Warwick") (established in the 1960s), the founder members of the group were all universities or university colleges prior to World War I, including most of Britain's [ancient universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_university "Ancient university") and "[redbrick universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redbrick_universities "Redbrick universities")". In 1998, Cardiff University and King's College London joined the group.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-kclandcardiff-12)

In March 2001, the Russell Group decided against selecting a preferred option for the future funding of higher education, stating that endowments, a graduate contribution, increased public funding and top-up fees should all remain options.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-13) In December 2005, it was announced that the Russell Group would be appointing its first full-time director-general as a result of a planned expansion of its operations, including commissioning and conducting its own policy research.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-14) In November 2006, Queen's University Belfast was admitted as the twentieth member of the group.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-the91106-15) In the same month [Wendy Piatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Piatt "Wendy Piatt"), the then deputy director in the Prime Minister's strategy unit, was announced as the group's new Director General and chief executive.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-the91106-15)

In March 2012, it was announced that four universities – Durham, Exeter, Queen Mary University of London; and York – would become members of the Russell Group in August of the same year.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-bbc12312-10) All of the new members had previously been members of the [1994 Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Group "1994 Group") of British universities.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-bbc12312-10)

In January 2013, it was announced that the Russell Group would establish an academic board to advise the English exams watchdog [Ofqual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ofqual "Ofqual") on the content of [A-Levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GCE_Advanced_Level_(United_Kingdom) "GCE Advanced Level (United Kingdom)").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-16) In 2019, the group launched the website "Informed Choices" to advise school children on which A-level subject choices were useful for various degree courses, replacing an earlier teachers' guide of the same name from 2011 that had identified a list of "facilitating subjects'.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-18)

### Objectives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Objectives")]

The Russell Group states that "its aim is to help ensure that our universities have the optimum conditions in which to flourish and continue to make social, economic and cultural impacts through their world-leading research and teaching".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-About-3)

It works towards this by lobbying the UK government and parliament; commissioning reports and research; creating a forum in which its member institutions can discuss issues of common concern; and identify opportunities for them to work together.

## Members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Members")]

The Russell Group currently has twenty-four members,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-guardian2012-11) of which twenty are from England, two from Scotland, and one from each of Wales and Northern Ireland. Of the English members, five are from [Greater London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London "Greater London"); three from the [Yorkshire and the Humber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_and_the_Humber "Yorkshire and the Humber") region; two from each of the [North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England "North East England"), [North West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_West_England "North West England"), [West Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_(region) "West Midlands (region)"), [South West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_England "South West England") and [South East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_East_England "South East England") regions; and one from each of the [East Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Midlands "East Midlands") and [East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_of_England "East of England") regions. Four Russell Group members are constituent colleges of the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London") and a fifth London institution, Imperial College London, was part of the University of London until 2007.

## Status

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Status")]

### Research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Research")]

In 2022/23, following the 2021 [Research Excellence Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Excellence_Framework "Research Excellence Framework") (REF), the English universities of the Russell Group saw their share of recurring research funding from [Research England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_England "Research England") drop by 2.71 percentage points from the 2021/22 funding (based on the previous 2014 REF) to 68.21 per cent, although most institutions saw a rise in actual funding levels due to an overall increase in funding. The top 19 English institutions in terms of funding continued to all be from the Russell Group, with the top 20 being rounded off, as before, by [Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Lancaster "University of Lancaster"). The LSE was, as in previous REF rounds, the exception, ranking 31st in terms of funding (down from 23rd in 2021/11) and seeing a nine per cent fall (£1.7 million) in its allocation.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-22)

In 2015/16, following the 2014 REF, the 19 English universities with [HEFCE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HEFCE "HEFCE") research funding allocations (excluding transitional funding) in excess of £20 million were all members of the Russell Group. The only English Russell Group institution to receive an allocation below £20 million was the LSE (£18.6 million), which ranked 22nd behind the Universities of [Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Leicester "University of Leicester") and Lancaster (both on £19 million).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-23)

In 2010/11, 19 of the 20 UK universities with the highest income from research grants and contracts were members of the Russell Group.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-thefindat-24) In terms of total research funding allocations from the [Higher Education Funding Council for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_Education_Funding_Council_for_England "Higher Education Funding Council for England") (HEFCE) in 2007/8, the top 15 universities were all Russell Group institutions.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-education.guardian.co.uk-25)[LSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") was 21st, due to its focus on less costly social sciences research. [Queen's University Belfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_University_Belfast "Queen's University Belfast"), [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff_University "Cardiff University"), [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Glasgow "University of Glasgow") and [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Edinburgh "University of Edinburgh"), were not included in this table, as they are not English institutions. The Russell Group institutions received 82% of the total HEFCE research funding allocation.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-education.guardian.co.uk-25)

The research funding figures depend on factors other than the quality of research, in particular there are variations due to institutional size and subject spread (e.g. science, technology and medicine tend to attract more money).

In 2008, 18 of the then 20 members were positioned in the top 20 of [Research Fortnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Fortnight "Research Fortnight")'s [Research Assessment Exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Assessment_Exercise "Research Assessment Exercise") 'Power' Table. The other two places were occupied by [Durham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_University "Durham University") and [Queen Mary University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Mary_University_of_London "Queen Mary University of London"), which were not then Russell Group members but have since joined. The two Russell Group institutions outside the top 20 were QUB (21st) and the LSE (27th), while the other two universities to have since joined were York (22nd) and Exeter (25th).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-Research_Fortnight-26) In the equivalent table for the 2014 [Research Excellence Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Excellence_Framework "Research Excellence Framework"), the 24 Russell Group members occupied the top 24 positions, with the [University of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Lancaster "University of Lancaster") in 25th being the highest-ranked non-Russell Group university.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-Research_Fortnight_2014-27)

### Selectivity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Selectivity")]

All but two of the universities in the Russell Group are part of the [Sutton Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_Trust "Sutton Trust")'s group of 30 highly selective universities, the [Sutton 30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_Trust#Sutton_Trust_30 "Sutton Trust") (the absent members being Queen Mary University of London and Queen's University Belfast).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-34) The [Sutton 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_Trust#Sutton_Trust_13 "Sutton Trust") group of the 13 most highly selective universities only includes one non-Russell Group member, the [University of St Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_St_Andrews "University of St Andrews").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-35)

The top 10 by average [UCAS points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCAS_Tariff "UCAS Tariff") of new undergraduate students in 2021–22 included three non-Russell Group universities: St Andrews (1st: 212 points), [Strathclyde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Strathclyde "University of Strathclyde") (2nd: 210 points), and [Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Aberdeen "University of Aberdeen") (joint 10th with Durham: 185 points).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-Entry_Standards-36) The top 10 by lowest offer rate to new undergraduate students in 2024-25 included three non-Russell Group universities: St Andrews (4th; 30.0%), [St George's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George's,_University_of_London "St George's, University of London") (7th; 42.0%) and [University of the Arts London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Arts_London "University of the Arts London") (10th; 48.4%). The average offer rate, including conditional and unconditional offers, across 'higher tariff' UK institutions (as defined by [UCAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCAS "UCAS")) was 63.3% in 2024.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-offer_rate-37)

### Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Finances")]

The Russell Group accounted for 49.1% of the income of the higher education sector in the UK in 2013–14, having risen from 44.7% of the total in 2001–02. Over the same period the total income of Russell Group universities rose by 69.9% in real terms, compared to a sector average of 54.4%.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-39) Russell Group universities are also seen as "particularly creditworthy" due to their membership of the group, allowing them to borrow money at low interest rates.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-40)

The total annual income for Russell Group members for 2023/24 was £25.31 billion (2020/21 – £20.30 billion) of which £5.67 billion (2020/21 – £4.77 billion) was from research grants and contracts, with an operating surplus of £6.50 billion (2020/21 – £1.15 billion). Russell Group universities hold a total endowment value of £6.66 billion excluding colleges (2020/21 – £6.18 billion) and net assets of £41.08 billion (2020/21 – £31.52 billion). ## Criticisms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Criticisms")]

### 'Elite' status questioned

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 'Elite' status questioned")]

In a statement made in 2014 to the Higher Education Policy Institute, [David Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Watson_(academic) "David Watson (academic)") of the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") suggested that the Russell Group's claim to represent 24 'leading universities' was "a real stretch". In the context of the Russell Group's reputation in the sector, he continued: "particularly dangerous, I think, is the bottom half of the Russell Group...The problem with the Russell Group is that it represents neither the sector as a whole [nor], in many cases, the best of the sector". Performance in research intensity showed that there were dozens of other UK universities "above the bottom Russellers".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-65)

A [Durham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_University "Durham University") academic, Vikki Boliver, published a report in 2015 claiming that the prestigious position of the Russell Group was not based on evidence, but rather successful marketing. Only the universities of Oxford and Cambridge were significantly more elite than the majority of "old" universities when a grouping analysis was performed using data on academic selectivity, research activity, teaching quality, socio-economic exclusivity and economic resources. The other 22 members of the Russell Group sit in a second tier of universities along with 17 other "old" universities ([Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Aberdeen "University of Aberdeen"), [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bath "University of Bath")*, [Dundee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Dundee "University of Dundee"), [East Anglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_East_Anglia "University of East Anglia")*, [Goldsmiths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldsmiths,_University_of_London "Goldsmiths, University of London")*, [Heriot-Watt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heriot-Watt_University "Heriot-Watt University"), [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Kent "University of Kent"), [Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_University "Lancaster University")*, [Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Leicester "University of Leicester")*, [Loughborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough_University "Loughborough University")*, [Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Reading "University of Reading")*, [Royal Holloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Holloway,_University_of_London "Royal Holloway, University of London")*, [St Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_St_Andrews "University of St Andrews")*, [SOAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOAS,_University_of_London "SOAS, University of London")*, [Strathclyde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Strathclyde "University of Strathclyde"), [Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Surrey "University of Surrey")* and [Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sussex "University of Sussex")*), mostly comprising former members of the defunct [1994 Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Group "1994 Group") (shown by asterisks). Another 13 "old" universities and 54 ["new" universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_universities_(United_Kingdom) "New universities (United Kingdom)") made up a third tier, with a fourth tier of 19 "new" universities. Within each tier, the differences between the institutions were less significant than the differences between the tiers.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-67) This reflected an earlier result from 2010 that, when the ["Golden Triangle"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_triangle_(universities) "Golden triangle (universities)") universities (defined in the study as Oxford, Cambridge, Imperial, LSE, and UCL) were omitted, the remaining (then) members of the Russell Group were outperformed by the (then) members of the 1994 Group.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-68)

Ant Bagshaw from the Wonkhe think-tank has criticised the use of Russell Group membership as a proxy for selectivity in official Department for Education reports and statistics, as better measures of selectivity are available from UCAS data. He states that the idea that "Russell Group membership is synonymous with 'best'" is "persistent, but unverified". He also notes that this may lead to less scrutiny of the performance of non-Russell Group selective universities with respect to widening participation and improving access.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-69)

### Protectionism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Protectionism")]

The [Institute of Economic Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Economic_Affairs "Institute of Economic Affairs") has argued that the Russell Group acts out of protectionist interests. It is claimed that this will "restrict competition, discourage innovation and encourage inefficiency, thereby depriving students of lower prices and/or greater choice".[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-Stanfield-70)

### Sustainability

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Sustainability")]

The twenty-four universities in the Russell Group are responsible for around half of the Scope 1 and 2 carbon emissions of the UK university sector.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-71)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] The Group as a whole has been criticised for an inconsistent and inadequate response to the need to identify emissions and take reduction measures.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-72) An Environmental Sustainability Network was announced by the Russell Group in December 2019;[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-73) as of November 2021 no outcomes from this had been announced.

### Widening access

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Widening access")]

Analysis by the Labour Party in 2018 found that the number of students from disadvantaged areas has only increased by one percentage point since 2010.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-74)

In 2015, Durham academic Vikki Bolívar published a paper, _Lies, damned lies, and statistics on widening access to Russell Group universities_, criticising the statistical analysis in the Russell Group publication _Opening Doors_. This had said that "real progress has been made over the last few years" in widening access, but Bolívar highlighted four areas where the statistics used to justify this claim were misleading. She also pointed out that there was "a growing body of statistical research evidence which indicates that one important barrier to widening access at Russell Group universities is that applicants from less advantaged social backgrounds are less likely to be offered places at these universities than comparably qualified applicants from more advantaged social groups" that had not been mentioned in the Russell Group report.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-75)

The **Russell Group** is a self-selected association of twenty-four [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"). The group is headquartered in [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge "Cambridge") and was established in 1994 to represent its members' interests, principally to [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom") and [parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom "Parliament of the United Kingdom"). It was incorporated in 2007.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-About-3) Its members are often perceived as being the UK's best universities, which has been widely disputed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-4)

As of 2017,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit) Russell Group members receive over three-quarters of all university research grant and contract income in the United Kingdom.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-profile-5) Russell Group members award 60% of all doctorates gained in the United Kingdom.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-profile-5) In the 2021 [Research Excellence Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Excellence_Framework "Research Excellence Framework"), Russell Group universities accounted for 65% of all world-leading (4*) research conducted in the UK, and 91% of the Russell Group's research was judged to be world-leading (4*) or internationally excellent (3*).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-6) In the 2023 [Teaching Excellence and Student Outcomes Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teaching_Excellence_Framework "Teaching Excellence Framework") (TEF), of the 20 English Russell Group universities which were assessed, 7 hold gold awards (35%) and 13 silver (65%). This compares to proportions across 128 higher education institutions of which 29% hold gold, 62% silver, and 9% bronze.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-7) Their graduates hold 61% of all UK jobs that require a university degree, despite being only 17% of all higher education graduates.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-9)

The Russell Group is named after the location of the first informal meetings of the Group, which took place at the [Hotel Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimpton_Fitzroy_London_Hotel "Kimpton Fitzroy London Hotel") in [Russell Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Square "Russell Square"), London.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-bbc12312-10)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The Russell Group of universities was formed in 1994 by 17 British research universities – Birmingham, Bristol, Cambridge, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Imperial College London, Leeds, Liverpool, London School of Economics, Manchester, Newcastle, Nottingham, Oxford, Sheffield, Southampton, University College London and Warwick, who originally met at [Hotel Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotel_Russell "Hotel Russell") shortly before meetings of the Committee of Vice-Chancellors and Principals (now [Universities UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_UK "Universities UK")) in nearby [Tavistock Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tavistock_Square "Tavistock Square"), close to the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London") buildings and, particularly, [Senate House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_House_(University_of_London) "Senate House (University of London)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-bbc12312-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-guardian2012-11) With the exception of [Warwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Warwick "University of Warwick") (established in the 1960s), the founder members of the group were all universities or university colleges prior to World War I, including most of Britain's [ancient universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_university "Ancient university") and "[redbrick universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redbrick_universities "Redbrick universities")". In 1998, Cardiff University and King's College London joined the group.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-kclandcardiff-12)

In March 2001, the Russell Group decided against selecting a preferred option for the future funding of higher education, stating that endowments, a graduate contribution, increased public funding and top-up fees should all remain options.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-13) In December 2005, it was announced that the Russell Group would be appointing its first full-time director-general as a result of a planned expansion of its operations, including commissioning and conducting its own policy research.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-14) In November 2006, Queen's University Belfast was admitted as the twentieth member of the group.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-the91106-15) In the same month [Wendy Piatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Piatt "Wendy Piatt"), the then deputy director in the Prime Minister's strategy unit, was announced as the group's new Director General and chief executive.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-the91106-15)

In March 2012, it was announced that four universities – Durham, Exeter, Queen Mary University of London; and York – would become members of the Russell Group in August of the same year.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-bbc12312-10) All of the new members had previously been members of the [1994 Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Group "1994 Group") of British universities.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-bbc12312-10)

In January 2013, it was announced that the Russell Group would establish an academic board to advise the English exams watchdog [Ofqual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ofqual "Ofqual") on the content of [A-Levels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GCE_Advanced_Level_(United_Kingdom) "GCE Advanced Level (United Kingdom)").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-16) In 2019, the group launched the website "Informed Choices" to advise school children on which A-level subject choices were useful for various degree courses, replacing an earlier teachers' guide of the same name from 2011 that had identified a list of "facilitating subjects'.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-18)

## Organisation

### Objectives

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Objectives")]

The Russell Group states that "its aim is to help ensure that our universities have the optimum conditions in which to flourish and continue to make social, economic and cultural impacts through their world-leading research and teaching".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-About-3)

It works towards this by lobbying the UK government and parliament; commissioning reports and research; creating a forum in which its member institutions can discuss issues of common concern; and identify opportunities for them to work together.

### Leadership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Leadership")]

The Russell Group is led by Chief Executive Tim Bradshaw and chaired by [Chris Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Day_(hepatologist) "Chris Day (hepatologist)"), Vice-Chancellor of the University of Newcastle.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-Chair_Day-2)

## Members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Members")]

The Russell Group currently has twenty-four members,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-guardian2012-11) of which twenty are from England, two from Scotland, and one from each of Wales and Northern Ireland. Of the English members, five are from [Greater London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London "Greater London"); three from the [Yorkshire and the Humber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_and_the_Humber "Yorkshire and the Humber") region; two from each of the [North East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_East_England "North East England"), [North West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_West_England "North West England"), [West Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Midlands_(region) "West Midlands (region)"), [South West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_England "South West England") and [South East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_East_England "South East England") regions; and one from each of the [East Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Midlands "East Midlands") and [East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_of_England "East of England") regions. Four Russell Group members are constituent colleges of the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London") and a fifth London institution, Imperial College London, was part of the University of London until 2007.

## Status

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Status")]

### Research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Research")]

In 2022/23, following the 2021 [Research Excellence Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Excellence_Framework "Research Excellence Framework") (REF), the English universities of the Russell Group saw their share of recurring research funding from [Research England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_England "Research England") drop by 2.71 percentage points from the 2021/22 funding (based on the previous 2014 REF) to 68.21 per cent, although most institutions saw a rise in actual funding levels due to an overall increase in funding. The top 19 English institutions in terms of funding continued to all be from the Russell Group, with the top 20 being rounded off, as before, by [Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Lancaster "University of Lancaster"). The LSE was, as in previous REF rounds, the exception, ranking 31st in terms of funding (down from 23rd in 2021/11) and seeing a nine per cent fall (£1.7 million) in its allocation.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-22)

In 2015/16, following the 2014 REF, the 19 English universities with [HEFCE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HEFCE "HEFCE") research funding allocations (excluding transitional funding) in excess of £20 million were all members of the Russell Group. The only English Russell Group institution to receive an allocation below £20 million was the LSE (£18.6 million), which ranked 22nd behind the Universities of [Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Leicester "University of Leicester") and Lancaster (both on £19 million).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-23)

In 2010/11, 19 of the 20 UK universities with the highest income from research grants and contracts were members of the Russell Group.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-thefindat-24) In terms of total research funding allocations from the [Higher Education Funding Council for England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_Education_Funding_Council_for_England "Higher Education Funding Council for England") (HEFCE) in 2007/8, the top 15 universities were all Russell Group institutions.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-education.guardian.co.uk-25)[LSE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") was 21st, due to its focus on less costly social sciences research. [Queen's University Belfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_University_Belfast "Queen's University Belfast"), [Cardiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiff_University "Cardiff University"), [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Glasgow "University of Glasgow") and [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Edinburgh "University of Edinburgh"), were not included in this table, as they are not English institutions. The Russell Group institutions received 82% of the total HEFCE research funding allocation.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-education.guardian.co.uk-25)

The research funding figures depend on factors other than the quality of research, in particular there are variations due to institutional size and subject spread (e.g. science, technology and medicine tend to attract more money).

In 2008, 18 of the then 20 members were positioned in the top 20 of [Research Fortnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Fortnight "Research Fortnight")'s [Research Assessment Exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Assessment_Exercise "Research Assessment Exercise") 'Power' Table. The other two places were occupied by [Durham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_University "Durham University") and [Queen Mary University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Mary_University_of_London "Queen Mary University of London"), which were not then Russell Group members but have since joined. The two Russell Group institutions outside the top 20 were QUB (21st) and the LSE (27th), while the other two universities to have since joined were York (22nd) and Exeter (25th).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-Research_Fortnight-26) In the equivalent table for the 2014 [Research Excellence Framework](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_Excellence_Framework "Research Excellence Framework"), the 24 Russell Group members occupied the top 24 positions, with the [University of Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Lancaster "University of Lancaster") in 25th being the highest-ranked non-Russell Group university.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-Research_Fortnight_2014-27)

### Selectivity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Selectivity")]

All but two of the universities in the Russell Group are part of the [Sutton Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_Trust "Sutton Trust")'s group of 30 highly selective universities, the [Sutton 30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_Trust#Sutton_Trust_30 "Sutton Trust") (the absent members being Queen Mary University of London and Queen's University Belfast).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-34) The [Sutton 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutton_Trust#Sutton_Trust_13 "Sutton Trust") group of the 13 most highly selective universities only includes one non-Russell Group member, the [University of St Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_St_Andrews "University of St Andrews").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-35)

The top 10 by average [UCAS points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCAS_Tariff "UCAS Tariff") of new undergraduate students in 2021–22 included three non-Russell Group universities: St Andrews (1st: 212 points), [Strathclyde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Strathclyde "University of Strathclyde") (2nd: 210 points), and [Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Aberdeen "University of Aberdeen") (joint 10th with Durham: 185 points).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-Entry_Standards-36) The top 10 by lowest offer rate to new undergraduate students in 2024-25 included three non-Russell Group universities: St Andrews (4th; 30.0%), [St George's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_George's,_University_of_London "St George's, University of London") (7th; 42.0%) and [University of the Arts London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Arts_London "University of the Arts London") (10th; 48.4%). The average offer rate, including conditional and unconditional offers, across 'higher tariff' UK institutions (as defined by [UCAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCAS "UCAS")) was 63.3% in 2024.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-offer_rate-37)

### Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Finances")]

The Russell Group accounted for 49.1% of the income of the higher education sector in the UK in 2013–14, having risen from 44.7% of the total in 2001–02. Over the same period the total income of Russell Group universities rose by 69.9% in real terms, compared to a sector average of 54.4%.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-39) Russell Group universities are also seen as "particularly creditworthy" due to their membership of the group, allowing them to borrow money at low interest rates.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-40)

The total annual income for Russell Group members for 2023/24 was £25.31 billion (2020/21 – £20.30 billion) of which £5.67 billion (2020/21 – £4.77 billion) was from research grants and contracts, with an operating surplus of £6.50 billion (2020/21 – £1.15 billion). Russell Group universities hold a total endowment value of £6.66 billion excluding colleges (2020/21 – £6.18 billion) and net assets of £41.08 billion (2020/21 – £31.52 billion). ## Criticisms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Criticisms")]

### 'Elite' status questioned

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 'Elite' status questioned")]

In a statement made in 2014 to the Higher Education Policy Institute, [David Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Watson_(academic) "David Watson (academic)") of the [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") suggested that the Russell Group's claim to represent 24 'leading universities' was "a real stretch". In the context of the Russell Group's reputation in the sector, he continued: "particularly dangerous, I think, is the bottom half of the Russell Group...The problem with the Russell Group is that it represents neither the sector as a whole [nor], in many cases, the best of the sector". Performance in research intensity showed that there were dozens of other UK universities "above the bottom Russellers".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-65)

A [Durham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_University "Durham University") academic, Vikki Boliver, published a report in 2015 claiming that the prestigious position of the Russell Group was not based on evidence, but rather successful marketing. Only the universities of Oxford and Cambridge were significantly more elite than the majority of "old" universities when a grouping analysis was performed using data on academic selectivity, research activity, teaching quality, socio-economic exclusivity and economic resources. The other 22 members of the Russell Group sit in a second tier of universities along with 17 other "old" universities ([Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Aberdeen "University of Aberdeen"), [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bath "University of Bath")*, [Dundee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Dundee "University of Dundee"), [East Anglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_East_Anglia "University of East Anglia")*, [Goldsmiths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldsmiths,_University_of_London "Goldsmiths, University of London")*, [Heriot-Watt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heriot-Watt_University "Heriot-Watt University"), [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Kent "University of Kent"), [Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_University "Lancaster University")*, [Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Leicester "University of Leicester")*, [Loughborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough_University "Loughborough University")*, [Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Reading "University of Reading")*, [Royal Holloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Holloway,_University_of_London "Royal Holloway, University of London")*, [St Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_St_Andrews "University of St Andrews")*, [SOAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOAS,_University_of_London "SOAS, University of London")*, [Strathclyde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Strathclyde "University of Strathclyde"), [Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Surrey "University of Surrey")* and [Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sussex "University of Sussex")*), mostly comprising former members of the defunct [1994 Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Group "1994 Group") (shown by asterisks). Another 13 "old" universities and 54 ["new" universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_universities_(United_Kingdom) "New universities (United Kingdom)") made up a third tier, with a fourth tier of 19 "new" universities. Within each tier, the differences between the institutions were less significant than the differences between the tiers.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-67) This reflected an earlier result from 2010 that, when the ["Golden Triangle"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_triangle_(universities) "Golden triangle (universities)") universities (defined in the study as Oxford, Cambridge, Imperial, LSE, and UCL) were omitted, the remaining (then) members of the Russell Group were outperformed by the (then) members of the 1994 Group.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-68)

Ant Bagshaw from the Wonkhe think-tank has criticised the use of Russell Group membership as a proxy for selectivity in official Department for Education reports and statistics, as better measures of selectivity are available from UCAS data. He states that the idea that "Russell Group membership is synonymous with 'best'" is "persistent, but unverified". He also notes that this may lead to less scrutiny of the performance of non-Russell Group selective universities with respect to widening participation and improving access.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-69)

### Protectionism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Protectionism")]

The [Institute of Economic Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Economic_Affairs "Institute of Economic Affairs") has argued that the Russell Group acts out of protectionist interests. It is claimed that this will "restrict competition, discourage innovation and encourage inefficiency, thereby depriving students of lower prices and/or greater choice".[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-Stanfield-70)

### Sustainability

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Sustainability")]

The twenty-four universities in the Russell Group are responsible for around half of the Scope 1 and 2 carbon emissions of the UK university sector.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-71)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] The Group as a whole has been criticised for an inconsistent and inadequate response to the need to identify emissions and take reduction measures.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-72) An Environmental Sustainability Network was announced by the Russell Group in December 2019;[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-73) as of November 2021 no outcomes from this had been announced.

### Widening access

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Russell_Group&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Widening access")]

Analysis by the Labour Party in 2018 found that the number of students from disadvantaged areas has only increased by one percentage point since 2010.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-74)

In 2015, Durham academic Vikki Bolívar published a paper, _Lies, damned lies, and statistics on widening access to Russell Group universities_, criticising the statistical analysis in the Russell Group publication _Opening Doors_. This had said that "real progress has been made over the last few years" in widening access, but Bolívar highlighted four areas where the statistics used to justify this claim were misleading. She also pointed out that there was "a growing body of statistical research evidence which indicates that one important barrier to widening access at Russell Group universities is that applicants from less advantaged social backgrounds are less likely to be offered places at these universities than comparably qualified applicants from more advantaged social groups" that had not been mentioned in the Russell Group report.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Group#cite_note-75)
